name: Ground-to-air signals
summary: Huge, straight, high-contrast symbols in an open place — the international codes an aircrew is trained to read.

steps.text: Choose the biggest open, flat area you can reach that is visible from above.
Make each symbol at least 3 m of stroke length and 6 m if you can — bigger than feels necessary. Make the strokes wide as well as long.
steps.why: An aircraft searching at altitude and speed has seconds over you. Small or thin marks vanish into ground texture.

steps.text: Use whatever contrasts most with the ground: dark branches on snow, stones on grass, trampled and shadowed trenches in snow.
Lay the code you need: V = assistance required. X = require medical assistance. -> = proceeding this way. Y = yes. N = no. SOS also works.
Keep the strokes straight and the angles sharp — nature does not make straight lines, and that is exactly what makes it read as human.
If you have colour or reflective gear, lay it out too, and stand clear of the symbol waving something bright when an aircraft comes over.

verify: Walk 50 m away and look back. If you cannot instantly read it from there, it will not read from 300 m up.
In snow, dig the trenches deep enough to cast a shadow — shadow reads better from the air than colour does.
limits: It only works if someone is looking, in daylight, in weather they can fly in. It is one signal among several, not a plan on its own.
It cannot tell anyone where you are going once you leave it.
cautions: Do not walk all over the symbol afterwards — footprints blur the edges that make it legible.
If you move on, leave a marker showing the direction of travel, and the date.
